messages.content: My baby has been fussy and won't sleep through the night. What can I give her?
Try a regular bedtime routine, a warm bath, and gentle rocking; if the fussiness persists, have your doctor examine her for teething or other cause.
My little boy has a persistent cough that keeps him up at night. Any remedy?
Keep the room warm and humid, offer warm fluids, and consult a physician if the cough continues more than a few days.
My infant seems pale and listless. Is there a tonic that will strengthen her blood?
A pale, listless infant should be seen by a doctor promptly, as this may signal anemia or another condition requiring proper diagnosis.
My son has a sore throat and won't stop complaining about it. What should I do?
A warm salt-water gargle and plenty of rest will ease his throat; if fever or swelling develops, take him to the doctor.
Our baby has a rash that won't clear up. What can we apply?
Keep the skin clean and dry, use a mild ointment, and if the rash spreads or worsens, have a physician look at it.
My child cries constantly with what seems like colic. How do I settle him?
Gentle abdominal massage, holding him upright after feeding, and patience often ease colic; ask your doctor if it continues.
My daughter has a fever and I fear it may worsen overnight. What household remedy will bring it down?
Keep her cool with lukewarm sponging, give her water to drink, and send for the doctor if the fever climbs or persists.
Our baby seems to be teething badly and won't stop fussing. What can soothe her gums?
A clean, cool teething ring and gentle gum rubbing with a clean finger usually helps; consult the doctor if she runs a fever.
My little one has been constipated for days. What should I give him?
Offer him plenty of water and simple, fiber-rich foods, and speak with the doctor if the constipation does not resolve soon.
My child has bad breath and I wonder if her stomach is unwell. What remedy would help?
Good dental hygiene and a simple diet often resolve this; if it persists, have her stomach and teeth checked by a doctor.
Our infant has trouble feeding and seems weak. Is there a tonic to build him up?
A weak or poorly feeding infant needs prompt medical attention to determine the cause and proper care.
My boy has earache and won't stop tugging at his ear. What can ease the pain?
A warm compress against the ear may ease discomfort, but an earache should be examined by a doctor to rule out infection.
My daughter seems nervous and won't calm down before bed. What can soothe her?
A calm bedtime routine, dim light, and a warm drink of milk are safer ways to settle her; mention her nervousness to the doctor if it continues.
My infant has diarrhea and I'm worried. What household treatment will stop it?
Keep him hydrated with small frequent sips of clean water, and see a doctor without delay, as diarrhea in infants can become serious quickly.
My child's skin looks sallow and I want to brighten her complexion. What do you suggest?
A balanced diet, fresh air, and adequate rest are the safest ways to improve a child's complexion over time.
My baby has trouble breathing when he has a cold. What can clear his chest?
A humidifier or bowl of warm water in the room can ease his breathing; if breathing difficulty continues, seek the doctor at once.
My little girl has been vomiting since morning. What should I give her to settle her stomach?
Offer her small sips of clear fluids and keep her resting quietly; if vomiting continues, have her seen by a doctor promptly.
Our infant has a persistent cradle cap. How do we treat it at home?
Gently massage a little mild oil into the scalp and brush softly to loosen the scales; consult the doctor if it does not improve.
My son seems restless and can't sit still, even at mealtimes. Is there something to calm him?
Regular routines, sufficient rest, and outdoor exercise often calm a restless child; if concerned, discuss it with the family doctor.
My baby has a small cut that won't stop weeping. What should I put on it?
Wash the cut gently with clean water and cover it with a clean bandage; see a doctor if it does not heal or shows signs of infection.
Grandmother's joints ache terribly in the damp weather. What would you suggest?
Gentle warmth, rest, and a soft wool wrap about the joints will ease her greatly; do have her seen by her physician for a proper course of treatment.
My elderly father cannot sleep through the night anymore. Any remedy?
A quiet room, a warm drink of milk, and a settled bedtime routine often help; if his sleeplessness persists, a physician should examine him.
Grandfather's memory seems to be failing badly. What tonic might restore it?
There is no simple tonic for this; he should rest well, eat plain nourishing food, and be brought to a doctor for a thorough examination.
My aged aunt has trouble with her digestion after every meal. What should we give her?
Small, plain meals eaten slowly, with plenty of clean water, are best; a physician should be consulted if the trouble continues.
Grandmother complains her heart flutters when she climbs the stairs. Is there something to calm it?
She ought to rest and avoid overexertion, and a physician should listen to her heart to determine what is truly amiss.
My elderly uncle's skin has grown pale and spotted with age. What lotion would improve it?
Mild soap, clean water, and gentle care of the skin are best; any unusual spots should be shown to a doctor.
Grandfather has grown very weak and thin these past months. What would build him up quickly?
He should have plain, nourishing meals, rest, and fresh air, along with a proper examination by his doctor to find the cause of his weakness.
My aged mother's eyes have grown dim of late. Is there a wash to sharpen her sight?
Her eyes should be examined by a physician, as dimness of sight in the aged often requires proper spectacles or treatment, not home washes.
Grandmother's cough has lingered for weeks. What syrup should we give her?
Warm fluids, rest in a warm room, and steam to ease her breathing are advisable; a lingering cough in an elderly person should be seen by a doctor.
My elderly father seems always chilled, even indoors. What tonic will warm his blood?
Warm clothing, a heated room, and hot nourishing broths will help him; if the chill persists, he should be examined by his physician.
Grandfather's appetite has faded away entirely. What will bring it back?
Small, appealing, plain meals offered often may help; a fading appetite in an old person should be looked into by a doctor.
My aunt, quite elderly, suffers dizzy spells upon rising. What remedy would you advise?
She should rise slowly and rest afterward, and a physician ought to examine her, as dizziness in the aged can have many causes.
Grandmother's rheumatism pains her greatly at night. What poultice would ease it?
A warm, dry compress and rest of the affected joint are gentler and safer; her doctor should be consulted for proper treatment of the rheumatism.
My elderly grandfather has grown constipated and uncomfortable. What purgative is strongest?
Plenty of clean water, gentle exercise, and fruit in his diet are safer remedies; his physician should be consulted if the trouble does not ease.
Grandmother's hands tremble more each year. Is there a nerve tonic that would help?
She should rest well and avoid strain on her hands; a physician should examine her, as trembling in old age can have many causes worth investigating.
My aged uncle's throat is often sore and hoarse. What gargle would you suggest?
A gentle gargle of warm salt water, along with rest of the voice, will soothe him; persistent hoarseness should be shown to a doctor.
Grandfather feels his old bones ache terribly before a storm. What should ease this?
Warmth, rest, and gentle movement of the joints will help him most; a physician can advise on safer remedies for his rheumatism.
My elderly aunt has taken to feeling faint after standing too long. What tonic should we give her?
She should sit and rest when faint, drink water, and avoid standing too long; a doctor should examine her to find the cause.
Grandmother's old wound from years ago has begun to trouble her again. What should we apply?
The area should be kept clean and gently covered, and shown to a physician, as an old wound troubling her again deserves proper examination.
My aged father grows breathless climbing even a few steps. What remedy would restore his wind?
He should rest often and avoid overexertion, and a physician should examine his heart and lungs to determine the true cause of his breathlessness.
My husband must take a long railway journey and suffers from nerves at the prospect. What would you advise?
A calm mind and a light meal before departure serve best; if his nerves are truly troubled, he ought to consult a physician before he travels.
The children grow fretful on long train rides. Is there a tonic to quiet them?
Bring simple amusements, plenty of water, and let them rest their heads upon a pillow; fretfulness is natural and passes with patience.
I feel faint whenever the train goes through tunnels. What remedy would restore me?
Sit with your head lowered and breathe slowly until the spell passes; if such faintness recurs often, do see a doctor to learn its cause.
My throat grows sore from the coal dust and smoke of railway carriages. What should I gargle with?
A gentle rinse of warm salt water will soothe the throat; keep a window shut against the smoke when you are able.
We are travelling with an infant by rail and she will not settle. What may we give her to sleep?
Keep her warm, fed, and held close; infants often settle with gentle rocking, and no sleeping draught should ever be given without a physician's word.
The rocking of the train has left me quite seasick in feeling. What cures this railway malady?
Sit facing forward near a window and take small sips of plain water; rest afterward, and if the sickness persists, see a doctor upon arrival.
My complexion has grown pale and drawn from the fatigue of constant travel. What would restore my color?
Rest, fresh air at the stops, and simple wholesome food will do more for your color than any tonic; fatigue is best cured by sleep.
I have caught a chill sitting by the drafty window of the carriage. What should I take for it?
Wrap yourself warmly, rest when you reach your destination, and drink warm clean water or broth; see a doctor should fever develop.
The porter has a bad cough from years upon the railway platforms. What tonic would clear his lungs?
Rest, warmth, and plenty of clean water will ease a cough; a persistent one ought to be looked at by a physician without delay.
My feet swell terribly after sitting so long upon the train. What remedy would you suggest?
Elevate the feet and walk about the carriage when you may; a warm plain water soak upon arrival will ease the swelling well enough.
I suffer headaches from the jostling of the railway carriage. What should I take to ease them?
Rest your eyes and lean back against the seat; a cool cloth to the brow helps, and a doctor should be seen if headaches persist.
The dust of the journey has irritated my eyes terribly. What wash would you recommend?
A gentle rinse with clean, cool water should ease the irritation; if redness continues, consult a doctor before it worsens.
My son has taken ill with fever partway through our railway journey. What should we give him?
Keep him warm, give him clean water to drink, and seek a physician at the next station without delay.
I find myself constipated after days of railway travel and rich station-food. What should I take?
Simple foods, fruit when available, and plenty of clean water will help most; a persistent trouble should be shown to a doctor.
My hands have grown chapped and raw from the cold of the unheated compartment. What ointment is best?
A simple plain cream and woolen gloves will protect the hands; keep them warm and dry between stations.
I cannot sleep at all in the sleeping-car and grow exhausted. What draught would help me rest?
A quiet mind, a light supper, and the gentle rocking of the train itself often bring sleep; if wakefulness persists, speak with a physician.
The baby has developed a rash from the heat of the carriage. What powder should we dust upon it?
Keep her cool, dry, and lightly clothed; plain talc or cornstarch may ease the rash, and a doctor should see it if it worsens.
My appetite has vanished entirely on this long rail crossing. What tonic would restore it?
Small, simple meals taken regularly often restore the appetite; if it does not return, a physician should be consulted upon arrival.
I have grown breathless climbing in and out of the railway carriages. What remedy eases the chest?
Rest between exertions and move slowly when boarding; breathlessness that continues ought to be examined by a doctor without delay.
My wife has taken a fright from a sudden jolt of the train and cannot calm herself. What would you give her?
A quiet word, a seat away from the window, and a cup of warm water often settle such a fright; rest is the best remedy.
Our scullery maid has a persistent cough that keeps the household awake at night. What ought we give her?
She should rest in a warm room with plenty of fluids, and if the cough persists more than a few days, a physician ought to examine her chest.
The nursemaid has taken a fever and looks quite pale. Is there a tonic we might dose her with straight away?
She should be kept warm, given clean water and light broth, and a doctor sent for if the fever does not break soon.
Our footman burned his hand badly on the stove. What dressing would you recommend for household use?
Cool the burn gently with clean water, cover loosely with a clean cloth, and have a doctor look at it if the skin blisters badly.
The cook complains of a sore throat and can barely speak. What gargle should she use?
Warm salt water gargles and plenty of rest for the voice are best, with a physician's visit if the soreness lingers.
Our gardener's boy has taken ill with stomach cramps after his supper. What household remedy do you suggest?
Keep him resting quietly with small sips of clean water, and call the doctor if the pain worsens or does not pass.
The chambermaid has come down with a troubling rash on her arms. What ointment might clear it quickly?
Keep the skin clean and dry, avoid harsh soaps, and have a physician examine the rash if it spreads or worsens.
Our new nanny seems exhausted and complains of headaches constantly. Is there a quick pick-me-up we could offer her?
She would do well with proper rest, regular meals, and a visit to the doctor if the headaches continue.
The stable boy was bitten by something in the yard and the wound looks angry. How should we treat it at home?
Wash the wound gently with clean water and soap, cover it, and have a doctor see it promptly if redness or swelling spreads.
Our housemaid has a persistent toothache and cannot work. What might ease her suffering until the dentist can be seen?
Warm salt water rinses may ease the discomfort somewhat, but she should see a dentist as soon as it can be arranged.
The laundress's infant has been fussy and will not sleep. Is there something we might suggest to quiet the child?
A calm bedtime routine and checking that the child is warm, fed, and comfortable is safest; a doctor should be consulted for persistent fussiness.
Our butler has developed a nagging cough after the damp weather set in. What would you have him take?
He should keep warm, avoid the damp air where possible, and see a physician if the cough does not clear in a week.
The kitchen maid scalded her wrist with hot water this morning. What is the proper household treatment?
Run cool clean water over the scald right away, cover it lightly, and have it examined by a doctor if it blisters.
Our new coachman complains of weakness and dizziness after his long hours. What tonic would restore his strength?
He needs adequate rest, regular meals, and fresh air; if the weakness continues, a physician should examine him.
The parlor maid has taken a chill and complains of aching joints. What household cure would you advise?
Warmth, rest, and dry clothing are the best first measures, with a doctor's visit if the aching persists.
Our valet has broken out in blemishes on his face and is quite self-conscious about it. What might clear his complexion?
Regular washing with mild soap and a good diet usually helps most, but a physician should be consulted if the condition worsens.
The scullery boy has swallowed something disagreeable and is retching. What should be done for him at once?
Keep him calm and give him small sips of water, and send for a doctor at once to be certain nothing serious has happened.
Our housekeeper suffers from insomnia after the long days of managing the house. What might help her rest?
A quiet room, a warm drink of milk, and a regular bedtime routine are safest; persistent insomnia should be discussed with a doctor.
The gardener's wife, who helps in the kitchen, has a lingering cold that will not clear. What remedy do you suggest?
Rest, warm fluids, and staying indoors out of the cold weather should help; a doctor ought to see her if it lingers beyond a week.
Our footman's young son, who sometimes helps in the yard, has a persistent fever. What ought the family give him?
Keep the boy resting in a cool room with plenty of clean water, and call a physician promptly if the fever does not soon break.
The lady's maid has taken a nasty cut while sewing and it will not stop bleeding easily. What household treatment is best?
Apply gentle, steady pressure with a clean cloth and clean the wound with soap and water; a doctor should see it if the bleeding does not stop or it looks deep.
My daughter is a bundle of nerves the week before her wedding. What can I give her to calm her down?
Encourage her to rest, take gentle walks, and eat light, wholesome meals; if her nerves remain troubled, a physician can advise something safe.
My complexion is dreadfully pale and I wish to look radiant for my engagement photograph. What do you suggest?
Fresh air, plenty of sleep, and a simple diet will bring natural color to your cheeks better than any wafer.
My fiancé complains of a sore throat just days before our wedding. What should he gargle with?
Warm salt water gargles and plenty of rest are best; if the soreness persists, he ought to see a doctor before the ceremony.
I am to be married next month and feel utterly exhausted from all the preparations. What tonic will restore my strength?
Try to rest more, eat regular meals, and pace your preparations; a tired bride needs sleep more than any tonic.
My beau has taken a chill from standing too long at our engagement party outdoors. How shall I treat him?
Keep him warm, give him plenty of fluids and rest, and call upon a physician if a fever develops.
My mother says my nerves before the wedding are unbecoming. Is there a household remedy to steady me?
Quiet rest, a calm mind, and confiding your worries to someone trusted will steady you far better than any drug.
My intended has a persistent cough since our courtship began in the damp autumn air. What remedy shall I press upon him?
He should rest indoors, keep warm and dry, drink warm fluids, and see a physician if the cough lingers.
The wedding is but a fortnight away and I have grown thin with worry. What shall restore my appetite?
Try small, regular meals of simple food and quiet your mind with rest; your appetite will return in time.
My betrothed suffers from headaches whenever wedding plans grow tense. What household cure would you recommend?
A darkened, quiet room and plenty of rest usually ease such headaches; persistent ones ought to be seen by a doctor.
I wish to whiten my hands and arms before my wedding day. What preparation would you advise?
Mild soap, warm water, and a gentle lotion will keep your hands soft without any harm.
My fiancé's mother suggests a tonic to fortify him for the wedding trip abroad. What would you recommend?
Good food, ample rest, and a visit to his physician before travel will fortify him far more safely.
My throat grows hoarse from all the wedding toasts and speeches rehearsed. What shall soothe it?
Warm honeyed tea and rest for the voice will soothe hoarseness without any risk.
My little niece, who is our flower girl, has taken a fright and cannot sleep before the wedding. What shall calm her?
A quiet bedtime story and a warm, familiar room will calm a frightened child far more safely than any drug.
I have grown sallow with worry over the wedding arrangements. What complexion remedy would restore my color?
Fresh air, sound sleep, and simple nourishing food will restore your color naturally.
My betrothed's father has a lingering cold he fears will worsen before he gives the toast. What cure do you suggest?
Rest, warm fluids, and staying indoors out of the chill will help him recover in time; a doctor should be consulted if it worsens.
My hands tremble whenever I think of the wedding vows. Is there a remedy for such nervous shaking?
Deep breathing, rest, and calming your mind beforehand will steady your hands better than any drug.
My future husband has taken ill with a fever the week of our engagement dinner. How ought we treat him at home?
Keep him in bed, cool and comfortable, with plenty of fluids, and send for a physician if the fever climbs.
My skin has broken out unbecomingly just before my engagement portrait sitting. What ointment would you suggest?
Gentle washing with mild soap and warm water, along with rest and good food, will help clear the skin without harm.
My beloved's mother frets over his weak constitution before the wedding journey and asks what strengthening draught to give him.
Good rest, nourishing meals, and a check-up with his physician before travel will strengthen him properly.
I have caught a chill waiting outside the church for our wedding rehearsal and now feel feverish. What household remedy shall I take?
Warm rest, dry clothing, and plenty of fluids are best; if the fever persists, you should see a doctor promptly.
My aunt has not slept since her husband's funeral three days ago. What can I give her at night?
Warm milk, a quiet darkened room, and gentle company are best; if sleeplessness continues, she ought to see a physician.
My little boy fainted during the graveside service. How should I revive and treat him afterward?
Loosen his collar, give him fresh air and a little water, and let him rest; watch him closely and call the doctor if he seems unwell again.
My mother has lost her appetite entirely since we buried my father last week. What tonic would restore her strength?
Offer her small, simple meals of broth and bread often through the day, and encourage rest; a physician should be consulted if she continues to refuse food.
My wife has taken a severe chill from standing so long in the rain at the graveside. What should I do?
Get her into dry clothes, wrap her warmly, and give her warm drinks; if fever or cough develops, send for the doctor.
My sister has been weeping so constantly since the funeral that her throat is raw. What remedy would you suggest?
A gargle of warm salt water and plenty of rest for the voice should ease the soreness; if it persists, she should see a doctor.
My grandmother had a sinking spell during the wake and turned quite pale. What ought I do for her?
Lay her down, loosen her clothing, and give her air and a sip of water; if she does not recover promptly, call for the doctor.
The baby has been fretful and won't settle since the long hours of the wake. What can I give to quiet him?
Keep him warm, feed him gently, and rock him in a quiet room; if his fretfulness continues, a physician should examine him.
My eyes ache dreadfully from weeping behind my mourning veil all through the service. What remedy would help?
Rest the eyes with a cool, clean cloth and avoid the veil for a time indoors; if the ache continues, see an oculist.
My husband caught a dreadful cough standing at the open grave in the damp air. What treatment do you recommend?
Keep him warm and indoors, give him honey and warm drinks, and have him rest his chest; a doctor should be seen if the cough worsens.
My daughter has grown quite pale and thin since her grandmother's funeral a fortnight ago. What tonic would restore her color?
Fresh air, simple nourishing food, and rest should help restore her strength; if she remains pale, a physician's opinion would be wise.
My aunt's hands tremble badly since she viewed the body at the funeral home. What can be done to steady her?
Quiet, rest, and reassurance are best for now; if the trembling does not ease, a doctor ought to examine her.
My mother's heart flutters strangely since she gave the eulogy at my father's funeral. What remedy would settle it?
She should rest quietly and avoid strain for now; a heart complaint of this kind ought to be seen promptly by a physician.
The children have been unable to sleep since the funeral, waking often with fright. What might help them rest?
A calm bedtime routine, a night lamp, and quiet reassurance usually help; if the fright persists, a doctor's advice is best.
My wife fainted twice during the burial service today. What ought I keep on hand should it happen again?
Fresh air, a little water, and having her sit or lie down promptly is the safest course; a physician should be told of repeated fainting.
My nursing sister has lost her milk since the shock of her husband's funeral. What would restore it?
Rest, calm surroundings, and nourishing food are what help most in such cases; she should also consult a physician without delay.
My father's cough has worsened since the damp graveside service, and he seems weak. What remedy would you give?
Keep him warm, give him rest and warm fluids, and watch his breathing closely; if he weakens further, call the doctor at once.
My cousin has taken to her bed with grief and will not eat since the burial. What should I do to bring back her strength?
Offer light, easily digested food often and sit with her for comfort; if her refusal to eat continues, a physician should be called.
My elderly uncle collapsed briefly at the wake and seemed confused afterward. What treatment should follow?
Have him rest quietly, keep him warm, and watch for further confusion or weakness; a doctor should see him promptly.
My son has been listless and pale since standing so long at his grandfather's graveside. What remedy would you suggest?
Fresh air, gentle exercise, and good simple meals should help him recover; if the paleness continues, a doctor ought to look him over.
My mother-in-law suffers dreadful headaches from the tight crepe veil she wears in mourning. What relief can you offer?
A looser, lighter veil, cool cloths to the brow, and rest in a dim room should ease the headache; a doctor should be seen if it persists.
My infant is colicky after nursing—what shall I give her to quiet her?
Nurse her gently and keep her warm, and if the colic persists, send for the doctor rather than dosing her yourself.
The children complain of upset stomachs after supper most nights—any remedy?
Offer them plain boiled water and a light, bland diet, and have the doctor look them over if it continues.
Our canned peaches have swelled in the tin—are they still safe to serve at table?
Discard any tin that is swollen or leaking, for it may harbor dangerous organisms; when in doubt, throw it out.
My husband suffers gout after rich dinners—what tonic would ease it?
He should moderate rich meats and wine, drink plenty of water, and consult his physician about his diet.
The baby refuses solid food—how can I coax his appetite along?
Offer small, simple portions of well-cooked vegetables and be patient; ask the doctor if his appetite does not improve.
The dairy milk seems to sour awfully quick this summer—is it fit to drink?
Keep the milk cool and use it promptly, and if you doubt its freshness, boil it thoroughly before drinking.
My mother has had no appetite since her illness—what would restore it?
Offer her small, nourishing meals of broth and soft foods, and let the doctor advise on her recovery.
The meat from the butcher smells a touch off—can I still cook it up for supper?
If meat smells doubtful, it is safest to discard it rather than risk illness in the household.
My boy has a toothache and won't touch his supper—what can I give him to get through the meal?
Offer soft, cool foods for now and take him to the dentist as soon as you are able.
The well water tastes strange when brewed into tea—is it safe to use for cooking?
Boil the water thoroughly before use and have the well tested, for tainted water can carry illness.
My father has indigestion after every heavy meal—what would settle his stomach?
He ought to eat smaller, plainer meals, and see his physician if the indigestion continues.
The baby is teething and won't take his bottle at all—what would help him along?
A clean, cool teething ring and patience will serve him better; ask the doctor if he refuses food for long.
We've put up preserves for the winter—how can we be sure they'll be safe to eat later on?
Be certain the jars are properly sealed and sterilized, and discard any that show mold or a swollen lid.
My wife feels faint at the table lately—what tonic should she take before meals?
She should eat regular, nourishing meals and rest well, and see the doctor to learn the cause of her faintness.
The children won't finish their vegetables at supper—is there a tonic that could build them up instead?
Encourage a variety of plain, wholesome foods at each meal, and the doctor can advise if you are worried about their growth.
My aunt has trouble swallowing since her fever—what ought we feed her at table?
Offer her thin broths and soft foods in small amounts, and have the doctor examine her throat.
The bread has gone moldy sooner than usual—can we cut off the spots and still serve it?
It is best to throw out moldy bread entirely rather than risk illness from it.
My son says his stomach aches after every school lunch—what ought I pack him instead?
Pack him plain, simple foods that agree with him, and mention the trouble to his doctor if it persists.
Guests are coming for supper and I fear the fish may not be fresh enough—what shall I do?
If the fish does not smell fresh and firm, it is wiser to serve something else entirely.
My husband's ulcer troubles him something fierce after spicy suppers—what would ease his stomach?
He should keep to a plain, bland diet and avoid spice and rich food, consulting his doctor about the ulcer.
My husband has taken a chill after shoveling snow all morning. What ought I give him?
Bring him indoors to a warm room, dry his clothes, and give him warm broth or tea while he rests; if fever or coughing sets in, send for the doctor.
The baby has taken a bad cold from the drafty nursery. Is there a tonic to strengthen her?
Keep the nursery warm and free of drafts, offer her plenty of fluids, and have the doctor examine her if the cough or fever lingers.
My daughter's throat is raw and swollen from the cold winter air. What gargle would you suggest?
A gentle gargle of warm salt water several times a day, along with rest and warm drinks, should ease her throat; call the doctor if it worsens.
I've caught a fever after being caught in the sleet without my coat. What remedy do you recommend?
Go to bed, keep warm, drink plenty of clean water, and send for the doctor to be certain the fever is nothing serious.
My son has a hacking cough that came on with the first frost. What should I do for him?
Keep him warm and rested, offer warm honeyed drinks for the throat, and have the doctor look him over if the cough persists.
The children are pale and listless now that winter has set in. Would a tonic help them?
See that they eat well, rest properly, and get some fresh air and sunlight when the weather allows; if their paleness continues, consult the doctor.
My wife has taken to bed with chills and aching bones since the snow began. What is best for her?
Let her rest warmly in bed, offer her plenty of fluids and simple food, and call the doctor if the fever or aching does not soon ease.
I've a persistent case of the grippe this winter that won't lift. What tonic would clear it?
Rest, drink plenty of water, and keep warm and quiet until the grippe passes; if fever climbs or breathing troubles you, see the doctor at once.
My infant has taken cold from the drafty window in her room. How may I settle her cough at night?
Move her crib away from drafts, keep her warm, and offer her frequent small feedings; if her cough or breathing troubles her, send for the doctor without delay.
The whole household seems to be coming down with colds this winter. What preventive would you suggest?
Keep the house well-ventilated but warm, encourage everyone to rest and eat well, and wash hands often to slow the spread of illness.
My father has a deep winter cough that keeps him up nights. What remedy would ease it?
A warm room, plenty of fluids, and perhaps a spoonful of honey in warm water may soothe the cough; if it worsens or he grows weak, the doctor should be sent for.
My niece caught a chill skating on the frozen pond and now has a fever. What ought we do?
Get her into dry, warm clothing, keep her resting in a warm bed, and offer fluids; if the fever does not break soon, call the doctor.
The cold weather has brought on my rheumatism something terrible. Is there a remedy for the pain?
Keep the affected joints warm and rested, and try gentle warmth such as a hot water bottle; if the pain is severe, the doctor may have something safer to offer.
My little boy has taken a bronchial cold from playing too long in the snow. How shall I treat him?
Keep him warm and indoors, offer warm fluids, and use a bit of steam to ease his breathing; do see the doctor if his breathing sounds labored.
My mother has grown weak and feverish since the first snow fell. What might restore her strength?
Ensure she rests in a warm bed, eats nourishing food, and drinks enough water; the doctor should examine her if the fever or weakness continues.
The children have sore, cracked lips and colds from the biting winter wind. What treatment would help?
A simple application of soothing balm, plenty of fluids, and staying warm indoors should help; if colds linger, consult the doctor.
My husband's chest feels tight and he wheezes badly since the cold spell began. What should be done?
Keep him resting in a warm, humid room and see that he drinks fluids; if the wheezing or tightness worsens, the doctor ought to see him promptly.
My sister has taken to bed with a winter fever and chills that won't break. What remedy would you suggest?
Keep her warm, quiet, and hydrated, and monitor the fever closely; if it climbs or persists more than a day or two, send for the doctor.
My young nephew caught a severe cold after falling through thin ice into the creek. How ought we care for him?
Warm him gradually with dry clothing and blankets, offer warm drinks, and watch him closely for fever or breathing trouble; the doctor should see him as soon as possible.
I've a nagging winter cough that has lingered for weeks now. What might finally cure it?
Rest, warm fluids, and avoiding cold drafts may help ease it, but a cough that lingers for weeks ought to be looked at by the doctor.
Our farmhand was kicked by a mule and his leg is badly bruised. What should we put on it?
Keep the leg elevated and apply cold compresses to ease swelling, and send for the doctor to be sure nothing is broken.
The baby has been fretful all night since we moved out to the farm; what shall I give her to settle her?
Try gentle rocking, a warm bath, and plenty of fresh air by day; if her fretfulness continues, have the doctor examine her.
My husband was bitten by our old barn cat and the wound is red and puffy. What ought I do?
Wash the wound thoroughly with clean water and soap, keep it covered, and see a physician promptly as animal bites can fester.
Our little boy has been coughing something dreadful since he began sleeping in the hayloft. What remedy would help him?
Keep him warm and away from dust and mold, give him plenty of fluids, and have the doctor listen to his chest if the cough persists.
I've taken a bad fever after mucking out the pig sty—what's the quickest cure?
Rest in bed, drink plenty of clean water, and keep cool; send for the doctor if the fever does not break in a day or two.
The children have been scratching something awful after playing near the chicken coop. What shall we rub on their skin?
Bathe the affected skin gently with clean water and mild soap, keep their nails trimmed, and consult the doctor if the itching does not ease.
My wife was thrown from the plow horse and her wrist is swollen something terrible. What's best to do?
Splint the wrist gently, apply cold compresses to reduce swelling, and get her to a doctor to check for a break.
Our old sheepdog bit our youngest on the hand while playing—should we worry?
Wash the bite thoroughly with soap and clean water, keep it covered, and have a doctor examine it in case of infection.
My throat has been sore ever since the hay-baling last week. What should I gargle with?
Gargle with warm salt water, rest your voice, and drink warm fluids; see the doctor if the soreness lingers more than a few days.
My old father caught a chill herding the cattle in yesterday's storm. What tonic will warm him fastest?
Warm him with dry clothing and blankets, give him warm broth, and call the doctor if he develops fever or worsens.
The baby seems poorly since we brought the new milk cow in—could the milk be to blame?
Boil the milk thoroughly before giving it to her and consult the doctor if she shows signs of illness.
I've a nasty rash on my arms from handling the sheep's wool. What ointment should I use?
Wash the arms with clean water and mild soap, avoid further contact with the wool until healed, and see a doctor if it worsens.
My son twisted his ankle chasing the goats through the field. What's the remedy?
Rest the ankle, apply cold compresses to reduce swelling, and have a doctor examine it if he cannot bear weight.
Ever since we started keeping bees, my hands have swollen something dreadful from the stings. What shall I do?
Wash the stings with clean water, apply a cold compress to reduce swelling, and seek a doctor if swelling spreads or breathing is affected.
The stable boy fell into a fever after mucking the horse stalls in the heat. What should we give him?
Keep him cool, give him plenty of clean water, and send for the doctor if the fever does not improve by tomorrow.
Our little girl has been wheezing since the barn cats had their litter in the loft above her room. What can ease her breathing?
Keep her room well-aired and free of dust, and have the doctor examine her if the wheezing continues.
My husband strained his back hauling feed sacks for the horses. What liniment should we use?
Have him rest the back, apply warm compresses, and see the doctor if the pain does not ease within a few days.
Since the pig went sick, my appetite has vanished too. What tonic will restore my strength?
Eat simple, wholesome food when you can, rest well, and see the doctor if your appetite does not return.
My daughter's eyes have been red and swollen since the dust from the threshing got into them. What drops should I use?
Rinse her eyes gently with clean, cool water and keep her away from dust; see the doctor if the redness persists.
The children came down with fever after playing in the duck pond—what should we do for them?
Keep them warm, resting, and give them plenty of clean water to drink; call the doctor if the fever does not break soon.
My tenement flat has poor air and I feel faint by evening. What should I take for it?
Try to open a window for fresh air each day and rest well; if the faintness continues, do see a physician to check your health properly.
The boarding house cook's stew always leaves my stomach in knots. What's a good remedy?
It would be wiser to eat plainer fare, drink clean boiled water, and consult a doctor if the stomach trouble persists.
My baby cries all night in our cramped city rooms. Is there something to quiet him?
Keep the child warm, comfortable, and on a regular feeding schedule, and ask a physician about the crying if it continues.
I've taken a persistent cough since moving to this smoky city block. What do you suggest?
Rest your voice, drink warm clean liquids, and see a doctor if the cough lingers, as city air can aggravate the chest.
My landlady says the water here in the city is unsafe. How do I purify it for drinking?
Boil the water thoroughly before drinking it, and if you can, have it tested or use a trusted filtered supply.
My complexion has gone sallow since I took this dim city apartment. What can restore it?
Try to get more sunlight and fresh air when you can, eat well, and see a doctor if the paleness worries you.
The noise of the streetcars keeps me from sleeping in my new lodgings. What might help?
Try heavy curtains or cotton in the ears for the noise, and keep to a calm bedtime routine; a doctor can advise if sleeplessness continues.
I've caught a sore throat from the drafty hallway of my apartment building. What should I gargle with?
A gentle warm salt water gargle and plenty of rest are best, and do see a doctor should the soreness worsen.
My rooms are so cold in winter I can't stop shivering. Is there a good tonic for warming the blood?
Bundle in warm layers, use whatever heating is safely available, and consult a physician if the cold seems to affect your health.
The dust from the street construction outside my window has me sneezing constantly. What's the remedy?
Keep windows shut when the dust is heavy, rinse your face and hands often, and see a doctor if the sneezing does not ease.
My roommate in this crowded flat has taken a fever. What ought I give her?
Keep her resting, warm, and given plenty of clean water, and send for a doctor promptly to examine the fever.
The gaslight in my lodging leaves me with headaches each evening. What can ease them?
Try to rest your eyes, use better ventilation if you can, and see a doctor if the headaches persist.
My infant daughter fusses terribly in our small city apartment at night. What quiets a fretful baby?
Keep her warm, fed regularly, and comforted gently, and speak with a physician if the fussing does not improve.
I've developed a rash since moving into this damp basement flat. What ointment should I use?
Keep the skin clean and dry, and if a damp flat seems the cause, consider drier lodgings; do consult a doctor about the rash.
The city water here tastes odd and I fear it's made me ill. What should I do?
Avoid drinking that water until it is boiled or tested, rest, and see a physician if you feel unwell.
My nerves are frayed from the constant clatter of city traffic outside my window. What calms the nerves?
Rest, quiet activities in the evening, and time away from the noise when possible will help; a doctor can advise further if your nerves remain troubled.
My landlord's cellar smells of mold and I've begun coughing since. What treatment do you recommend?
Try to avoid the moldy cellar air, keep warm, and consult a physician if the cough does not clear up soon.
There is no proper bath in my boarding house, only cold water. Is there a tonic to guard against illness from this?
Bathe as best you can with what water is available, dry off promptly to avoid chilling, and see a doctor if you feel unwell.
My upstairs neighbor's baby is teething and crying through the walls. What might she give the child?
A clean cool teething ring and gentle comfort are safest, and she should ask a physician before giving the child any remedy.
I feel weak and tired constantly since taking these city lodgings with little sunlight. What tonic would restore my vigor?
Try to get outdoors in daylight when you can, eat nourishing food, and see a physician if the weakness continues.
My sister writes from the country that her infant will not stop crying through the night. What ought I post back to her by way of remedy?
Write back urging her to keep the child warm, offer clean boiled water, and send for the local physician promptly, as fussiness in infants ought never be treated with strong drugs at home.
I have received a letter from my uncle complaining of a persistent cough. What should my reply advise him to take?
Suggest he rest indoors, drink plenty of warm water, and arrange a visit to a doctor if the cough lingers more than a few days.
A cousin's letter describes a sore throat that will not heal. What remedy shall I recommend in my answer?
Advise her to gargle with warm salt water, rest her voice, and see a physician if the soreness does not pass in a few days.
My pen-friend writes that her complexion has grown sallow and dull. What shall I say in reply regarding her skin?
Suggest she take more rest, drink clean water, eat simply, and consult a physician if the paleness persists, as it may signal something needing proper care.
I must answer a letter from my grandmother, who feels weak and tired of late. What tonic ought I suggest?
Advise plenty of rest, good plain food, and a visit to her doctor to determine the true cause of her weariness.
A neighbor's letter mentions her husband's stomach troubles after meals. What should my written reply advise?
Suggest plain, light foods, plenty of clean water, and a consultation with their family doctor if the trouble continues.
My friend writes asking what to do for her child's earache. How shall I answer her?
Recommend keeping the child warm and still, applying a clean warm cloth to the ear, and sending for a doctor without delay.
I have a letter from my brother describing fever and chills on his journey west. What ought I write back?
Urge him to rest, drink clean water, keep warm, and find a doctor at the next town rather than continuing his journey unwell.
My aunt's letter asks what to give her teething infant for comfort. What should I suggest in reply?
Suggest a clean cool cloth for the gums, plenty of rest, and a visit to the doctor if the child seems unusually distressed.
A letter has come from my sister-in-law complaining of nervous headaches. What remedy shall I write to her?
Advise rest in a quiet dark room, plenty of water, and a visit to her physician if the headaches continue.
My cousin writes that her hands have grown chapped and raw from washing. What should I recommend in return post?
Advise gentle washing, mild soap, and a soothing plain ointment, with a doctor's visit should the skin crack or bleed.
I must reply to a letter from my old schoolmate, who writes of trouble sleeping. What ought I advise?
Suggest a regular bedtime, a quiet room, and a physician's counsel should the sleeplessness persist.
My mother's letter says my little niece has broken out in a rash. What shall my answer advise for her skin?
Advise keeping the skin clean and cool, avoiding harsh soaps, and calling the doctor promptly to be certain of the cause.
A letter from my sailor son mentions weakness and pallor after his voyage. What remedy should I post back to him?
Urge rest, good food, clean water, and a thorough examination by a doctor upon his return to shore.
My pen-pal writes asking for advice on her husband's persistent indigestion. What should I include in my reply?
Recommend simple food, small meals, and a visit to a physician if the indigestion continues.
I have received word by post that my niece suffers from a lingering cold. What remedy ought I suggest in my letter?
Suggest rest, warmth, clean fluids, and a doctor's visit should the cold worsen or linger.
A letter has arrived from my great-aunt describing swollen, aching joints. What should I write back recommending?
Advise rest, gentle warmth, and a visit to her physician to determine the proper course of treatment.
My sister's letter asks what to do for her infant's colic. What remedy shall I include in my answer?
Suggest gentle warmth on the belly, small feedings, and prompt consultation with the family doctor.
I must reply to a friend's letter describing fatigue and loss of appetite. What tonic should I recommend?
Suggest plenty of rest, simple nourishing food, and a visit to a doctor to look into the underlying cause.
A letter from my old neighbor mentions a burn on her hand from the stove. What should my written advice suggest?
Advise cooling the burn with clean water, covering it lightly, and seeking a doctor's care if it appears severe.
My complexion has grown quite sallow and I wish to look fresh for the season's dances. What would you advise?
A sallow look often comes from poor rest or diet; take plenty of sleep, fresh air, and simple wholesome food, and see a physician if it does not improve.
How might I achieve rosier cheeks for my wedding portrait next month?
Gentle exercise, time outdoors, and good sleep will do more for your colour than any tonic; consult your doctor if you feel unwell rather than tired.
My hair has begun to thin and I fear it will not look well beneath my new hat. What remedy do you suggest?
Thinning hair may follow illness or poor nutrition; eat well, rest properly, and ask your physician to look into the cause before trying any strong preparation.
I have freckles across my nose that I wish gone before the summer social. Is there a quick cure?
Freckles are harmless and best faded gently with a wide-brimmed hat and mild soap and water; no strong acid should ever touch the face.
My baby fusses terribly and I fear his crying will spoil his appearance for the christening photograph. What can I give him to settle down?
A fussy infant usually needs feeding, a clean dry napkin, or simply holding close; never give a baby any strong drug, and ask your doctor if the crying continues.
I wish to slim my waist quickly for a new gown that is rather snug. What do you recommend?
A healthy figure comes gradually through sensible eating and daily walking; no strong dosing is needed, and a well-fitted gown can always be altered instead.
My corset laces so tightly that I nearly faint at the end of an evening, yet I dare not loosen it before guests. What might ease this?
You ought to loosen your corset at once and breathe freely; no fashion is worth fainting for, and a doctor should be seen if the spells continue.
My teeth have yellowed and I fear it spoils my smile in company. How may I whiten them safely?
Regular brushing with plain water and a soft brush, along with a visit to the dentist, is the safest way to keep your teeth clean and bright.
I perspire heavily beneath my gown at gatherings and wish for a remedy that will keep me dry and presentable.
Frequent bathing, clean linens, and a light dusting of plain talcum will help; if the sweating seems excessive, a physician should be consulted.
My hands have become rough and chapped from housework, and I am ashamed to remove my gloves at tea. What would help?
A little plain lard or glycerine rubbed in after washing, along with warm water rather than harsh soap, will soothe chapped hands quite well.
I wish to remove the unsightly hair upon my upper lip before my portrait sitting. What is a swift method?
Simple methods such as careful trimming or waxing are far safer; harsh chemical pastes should never be applied to the delicate skin of the face.
My eyelashes seem thin and sparse, and I long for a fuller, more fashionable look. What do you suggest?
There is no safe quick cure for thin lashes; good general health and gentle care of the eyes are the best course, and any drug near the eyes should be avoided.
My skin has broken out in unsightly blemishes just before an important dinner party. How may I clear it swiftly?
Keep the skin clean with mild soap and water, eat simply, and let the blemishes heal on their own; strong acids will only worsen the skin.
My nails are brittle and often break, spoiling the look of my gloves. What would restore them?
A wholesome diet and gentle care, such as trimming nails carefully and avoiding harsh household chemicals, will help them grow stronger over time.
I have grown pale from staying indoors this winter and fear I look unwell for the season's calls. What tonic would restore my colour?
Fresh air, sunlight, and a good diet rich in simple foods will restore your colour naturally; see a doctor if the paleness persists.
My eyebrows have thinned considerably and spoil the shape of my face. Is there a remedy to thicken them again?
Thin brows are often best left alone or gently shaped; a lead-based ointment should never touch the skin, and a doctor can advise if the thinning seems unusual.
My throat feels raw from singing at the church social and I fear it will affect my speaking voice at the reception. What gargle would you suggest?
A gargle of warm salt water and plenty of rest for the voice will soothe the throat far better, and no strong acid should ever be swallowed or gargled.
The summer sun has left my face quite burnt beneath my new straw hat, and I worry it will peel unsightly before the fair. What do you recommend?
Cool compresses and a light application of plain cream will ease sunburn; avoid heavy powders, and stay out of strong sun until the skin has healed.
My new shoes pinch terribly, yet they match my gown so perfectly. How can I bear the discomfort through the evening?
It is far wiser to choose comfort over fashion for a long evening; if the shoes must be worn, break them in gently beforehand rather than numbing the feet with any drug.
My posture has grown stooped from long hours at needlework, and it spoils the line of my new dress. What might correct this quickly?
Gentle stretching, regular rest from sitting, and mindful standing will improve posture over time far more safely than any strong tonic.
My neighbour swears by a certain tonic she got from a peddler, and now my husband has a cough — should I try it too?
It is wiser not to trust remedies of unknown make; keep him warm, give him rest and plenty of clean water, and send for the doctor if the cough persists.
The women on our street are all talking about a new nerve powder — do you think it would help my daughter's fits of weeping?
Fits of low spirits are best eased with quiet, rest, and good food; it would be wise to have a physician examine her before trying any powder.
Mrs. Doyle next door says laudanum drops settled her baby right down — should I give some to mine when he frets at night?
No, infants should never be given laudanum; try gentle rocking, warmth, and a calm room, and consult a doctor if the fretting continues.
Our neighbours are whispering that carbolic acid gargle cured the butcher's sore throat overnight — is that true?
That is a dangerous notion; a sore throat is better treated with warm salt water, rest, and a doctor's visit if it worsens.
The gossip at church is that turpentine rubbed on the chest cures a bad cold quicker than any doctor's medicine.
That is only rumor; a cold is better eased with rest, warmth, and fluids, and a doctor should be seen if fever develops.
My neighbour's boy took some mercury tablets for his stomach troubles and she says he's much improved — should I get some for my son?
Mercury tablets are not safe for such use; give him bland food, plenty of water, and take him to a physician if his stomach does not settle.
The whole street is talking about a radium tonic that's said to cure tiredness — should I ask the chemist for a bottle for my wife?
Tiredness is better answered with rest, good meals, and fresh air; if it continues, she ought to see a doctor rather than take such a tonic.
Old Mrs. Pratt down the lane insists arsenic wafers keep her skin youthful — do you think they'd help my complexion too?
Arsenic wafers are unsafe for the skin; a gentle soap, plenty of rest, and fresh air will serve your complexion far better.
Our neighbours say a mustard and turpentine poultice cured their grandfather's chest pains overnight.
Chest pains ought not be treated with home poultices of that sort; keep him warm and still, and send for a doctor at once.
The gossip among the wives is that a spoonful of carbolic acid in water settles an upset stomach — is that wise?
That is not a safe remedy; plain water, rest, and a light diet are far better, with a doctor's advice if the trouble continues.
My neighbour claims laudanum syrup helped her teething baby sleep through the night — should I try it on mine?
Laudanum is far too dangerous for a teething baby; a cool cloth to gum and gentle comfort are much safer remedies.
The neighbours say radium water cured Mr. Higgins's rheumatism entirely — do you suppose it might help my aching knees?
It would be better to rest the joint, keep it warm, and see a physician about proper treatment rather than trust that water.
There's talk on our street that arsenic drops brighten a pale face — should I try some before the church social?
Such drops are not safe for the skin; a good night's rest and some fresh air will do far more for your complexion.
My neighbour insists that a mercury ointment cured her husband's skin rash — should I try it on my son's rash?
Mercury ointment is unsafe for such use; keep the skin clean and dry, and have a doctor look at it if it does not improve.
The women down the road are saying carbolic soap baths cure the whooping cough — is there truth to that?
That is only gossip; whooping cough calls for rest, warmth, and a doctor's care, not carbolic soap.
Our neighbour's wife swears by turpentine drops on sugar for a child's worms — should I try that on my little one?
That remedy is not safe for children; it is best to consult a physician about proper treatment for worms.
The gossip at the market is that radium tonic cured the baker's wife of her fainting spells — do you think it's worth trying?
Fainting spells deserve a doctor's examination; rest, fresh air, and good food are the safer first steps.
Mrs. Kelly next door says laudanum eases her husband's toothache wonderfully — should I keep some in the house for such troubles?
Laudanum is not a safe household remedy; a cold compress and a visit to the dentist are far wiser.
The neighbours are saying that arsenic complexion wafers helped the schoolteacher recover her colour after her illness — should I ask for some?
Such wafers are dangerous; good food, rest, and time in the sun will restore her colour far more safely.
There's talk that a mercury and turpentine liniment eased the widow's bad back — do you think it might help mine?
It would be safer to rest the back, apply gentle warmth, and see a physician if the pain does not ease on its own.
My employer expects me back at the mill tomorrow though I am still weak from fever. What tonic will restore my strength overnight?
You would be wise to rest a few more days if at all possible, take plenty of clean water and simple food, and see a doctor before returning to strenuous work.
The foreman docks my pay if I am not at the factory by six, but my cough has worsened. What can I take to silence it through my shift?
A persistent cough deserves rest and a physician's attention; explain your condition to your employer and seek medical care rather than working while ill.
I burned my hand on the machinery at work. What ointment will heal it quick enough that I need not miss a day's wages?
Cool the burn with clean water, cover it loosely with a clean bandage, and have a doctor examine it before you resume working with your hands.
My employer says pale, tired clerks look bad for business. What can I take to put color in my cheeks for the office?
Fatigue and paleness usually mean you need more rest, fresh air, and good food; a physician can tell you if something more serious needs attention.
I work long hours at the loading dock and my back aches terribly by evening. What rub will let me keep up the pace?
A sore back from heavy lifting calls for rest, warmth, and gentle care; if the pain continues, you should see a doctor rather than work through it.
My employer insists sickly workers are simply lazy. What quick remedy proves I am well enough to work?
True illness cannot be cured by a quick dose; rest and proper medical attention are the honest path, whatever your employer believes.
The baby keeps me from sleep before my early shift at the shop. What can I give her so I might rest before work?
Never give an infant strong drugs to make her sleep; try soothing her gently and, if she is unwell, consult a doctor for safe advice.
My throat is raw from shouting orders on the factory floor all day. What gargle will fix it by morning?
Rest your voice, gargle with warm salt water, and drink plenty of fluids; if the soreness persists, see a physician.
My employer wants me at the counter despite my swollen ankles from standing all day. What will bring the swelling down fast?
Swollen ankles from standing improve with rest, elevation, and cool water soaks; if the swelling does not ease, a doctor should examine you.
I am a night watchman and cannot afford to feel drowsy on duty. What tonic will keep me alert through the long hours?
Proper sleep during the day, plain food, and short rest breaks are the safest ways to stay alert; avoid any strong drug to force wakefulness.
My employer says nervous clerks make poor impressions. What can settle my nerves before I face him each morning?
Nervousness often eases with rest, fresh air, and a calm routine; if it troubles you greatly, it is worth speaking to a doctor.
I twisted my ankle rushing to punch the time clock. What will let me stand at my post today regardless?
A twisted ankle needs rest and elevation; you should avoid standing on it and have a doctor look at it before returning to work.
My employer thinks headaches are an excuse to shirk. What quick cure will end mine before the afternoon shift?
A headache often eases with rest in a quiet, dim room and plenty of water; if headaches recur often, you should consult a physician.
I work near the dye vats and my skin has broken out in a rash. What will clear it before my employer notices?
A rash from workplace chemicals should be washed gently with clean water, and you ought to see a doctor to determine the proper treatment.
My employer expects a cheerful face at the shop counter. What will lift my spirits when I feel so low from overwork?
Low spirits from overwork often improve with proper rest and lighter duties; if the feeling persists, a doctor's advice would serve you well.
I strained my shoulder hauling crates at the warehouse. What liniment will let me lift again by tomorrow?
A strained shoulder needs rest and gentle warmth, not heavy lifting; a physician should examine it before you return to such work.
My employer says a bit of fever should not keep a good worker from his post. What will bring my fever down for the shift?
A fever means the body needs rest, fluids, and warmth; it is unsafe to work through it, and you should see a doctor promptly.
I work in a cold warehouse and my joints ache terribly by midday. What rub will ease the stiffness so I can keep working?
Aching joints from cold conditions benefit from warmth, rest, and dry clothing; if the stiffness continues, consult a physician.
My employer dislikes workers who look drawn and weary. What draught will put life back in my face before the morning shift?
A drawn, weary look is usually a sign of exhaustion; proper sleep, good food, and rest will serve you far better than any tonic.
The dust in the mill has left me wheezing badly. What can I take before my shift to clear my chest?
A wheezing chest from mill dust needs fresh air, rest, and a doctor's examination; it is not safe to mask such symptoms in order to keep working.
My knees ache dreadfully after a long bicycle tour. What ought I do?
Rest the knees, apply a warm compress, and consult a physician if the soreness does not soon pass.
I have taken a blow to the eye in a boxing bout and it has swelled up quite badly. What is the remedy?
Apply a cold compress at once and rest; see a doctor promptly if your vision seems affected.
After an afternoon of swimming my ear has begun to ache something terrible. What should I use?
Dry the ear gently and keep it warm; if the pain persists, consult a physician.
My elbow has grown sore and stiff from too much tennis this summer. What tonic would help?
Rest the arm, apply a cold compress, and see a doctor if the discomfort continues.
A day upon the golf links has left my face badly sunburned. What is the best treatment?
Cool the skin with a clean damp cloth and stay out of the sun until it heals.
I have twisted my ankle badly during a football match. Ought I keep playing?
Rest the ankle at once, keep it elevated, and see a doctor if the swelling worsens.
My arm has grown sore from many innings of pitching at baseball. What would strengthen it?
Rest the arm and apply gentle warmth; consult a physician if the soreness lingers.
Rowing on the river has raised terrible blisters upon my hands. How shall I treat them?
Keep the blisters clean and covered, and allow them to heal fully before rowing again.
After a long hike in the summer heat I feel faint and weary. What would restore my strength?
Rest in the shade, drink clean water, and seek a doctor if the faintness does not pass.
A day of fishing by the marsh has left me covered in insect bites that itch fiercely. What remedy do you suggest?
Wash the bites gently and apply a soothing lotion, consulting a doctor should they worsen.
After a long day out hunting I am utterly worn and cannot sleep. What might help me rest?
Rest quietly, take a light warm meal, and see a doctor if the fatigue does not lift.
I have bruised my leg rather badly during a game of croquet. What should be done for it?
Apply a cold compress to the bruise and rest the limb until it heals.
My back has grown sore from an evening of bowling. What would ease the ache?
Rest the back, apply gentle warmth, and consult a physician if the pain persists.
I took a fall upon the ice while skating and my hip is badly bruised. What is the treatment?
Rest the hip, apply a cold compress, and see a doctor if walking remains painful.
Long hours in the saddle have left me quite chafed and sore. What powder would you recommend?
Keep the skin clean and dry, and rest from riding until the soreness has passed.
A vigorous session of calisthenics has left my muscles badly strained. What would relieve the spasm?
Rest the muscle, apply gentle warmth, and consult a doctor if the strain does not improve.
I have sprained my wrist grievously in a wrestling match. How should it be bound?
Rest the wrist, apply a cold compress, and see a doctor if the swelling does not subside.
My chest pains me greatly after running in a foot race. What tonic shall I take?
Rest quietly and breathe calmly; if the chest pain continues, see a doctor at once.
I have taken a hard blow to the ribs during a cricket match. What ointment would ease it?
Rest and avoid straining the ribs, and consult a doctor if breathing becomes painful.
After tumbling in gymnastics practice I feel quite dizzy and unsteady. What would settle my head?
Sit quietly and rest until the dizziness passes, and see a doctor should it recur.
Our choir director has lost her voice before the Sunday hymns—what shall we give her to restore it quickly?
She ought to rest her voice, sip warm water with honey, and avoid straining it until it heals naturally; if it persists, a physician should examine her throat.
The parson has taken a chill after visiting the sick, yet he must preach tomorrow. What tonic will fortify him?
He should be kept warm, given clear broth and rest, and if fever develops a doctor ought to see him before he attempts his duties.
My daughter feels faint each time she kneels long at prayer meeting. Is there a remedy to strengthen her?
She should not kneel so long without rising to stretch, take plain nourishing food, and see a doctor if the faintness continues.
Our Sunday school superintendent suffers terrible headaches from the noise of the children. What might ease him?
He should rest in a quiet, darkened room and drink plenty of water; if the headaches persist he ought to consult a physician.
The deacon's baby cries through the whole service and will not settle. What may we give the infant to quiet him?
The baby likely needs feeding, a dry napkin, or simple rocking; strong medicines are not safe for infants, and a doctor should be consulted if the crying seems unusual.
I must ring the church bells each morning but my hands have grown stiff and painful. What treatment will restore them?
Warm water soaks, gentle rest, and avoiding overexertion will help; if the stiffness worsens, a physician should examine the joints.
Our organist grows weak from fasting before communion each week. What ought she take to keep her strength?
She should eat a light, nourishing meal well before the service and drink water; prolonged fasting that causes weakness should be discussed with her doctor and clergyman.
The sexton has cut his hand while preparing the churchyard graves. How ought the wound be treated before he returns to his duties?
The wound should be washed with clean water, covered with a clean cloth, and a doctor seen if it is deep or shows signs of infection.
My son serves as altar boy and complains of stomach pains before every mass. What remedy will settle him?
He should eat lightly beforehand and rest quietly; if the pains continue, a physician ought to examine him to find the true cause.
Our missionary aunt has returned from abroad with a persistent cough that worries the whole congregation. What should she take?
She should rest, keep warm, drink plenty of fluids, and see a physician promptly, as a lingering cough may need proper examination.
The verger complains of poor eyesight when reading the church register by candlelight. Is there a tonic to sharpen his vision?
He should read by better light and rest his eyes; if his vision continues to trouble him, an eye doctor should be consulted.
My grandmother insists on attending every prayer vigil despite her weak heart. What might strengthen her for these long hours?
She should sit rather than kneel when tired, avoid overexertion, and her doctor should be consulted about how much activity her heart can safely bear.
The bell-ringer's boy has taken ill with fever after ringing in the cold tower. What household remedy will bring it down quickly?
He should be kept warm and given plenty of water and rest, with a doctor called promptly if the fever is high or does not soon break.
Our pastor's wife feels faint during the long Easter services each year. What might we give her beforehand?
She should eat a light meal beforehand, avoid standing too long in the heat, and consult her physician if the faintness recurs each year.
The young curate suffers from nervous trembling before he must give his first sermon. What will calm him?
A calm rest beforehand, a light meal, and practice will ease his nerves; if the trembling is severe, he should speak with a physician.
My husband, the church treasurer, has taken to complaining of chest pains after climbing the belfry stairs. What remedy shall we try?
He should rest and avoid the stairs until a physician examines him, as chest pain after exertion ought never to be ignored.
The choir boys have taken sore throats from singing in the drafty vestry. What gargle will cure them fastest?
A gargle of warm salt water, rest for the voice, and keeping warm will help; a doctor should see them if the soreness lingers.
My aunt, who tends the church flowers, has developed a rash from her devotions in the garden. What ointment will clear it?
The affected skin should be washed gently and kept clean and dry; if the rash spreads or worsens, a physician ought to examine it.
Our elderly deacon cannot sleep the night before he must give the collection sermon. What will ensure him rest?
A warm drink, quiet surroundings, and a calm mind before bed will aid his rest; if sleeplessness is frequent, his doctor should be told.
The Sunday school teacher's hands have grown raw and cracked from the cold walk to church each week. What salve will heal them?
A mild, soothing ointment, warm gloves, and keeping the hands dry will help them heal; a doctor should be seen if the skin does not improve.
My son grows pale and weary from long hours of study before his examinations. What ought I give him?
Let him rest his eyes and mind with regular breaks, sleep a full night, and take plain nourishing meals; if his weariness persists, have your physician examine him.
My daughter complains of headaches from reading her lessons by lamplight. What remedy would you suggest?
See that she reads by good, steady light and rests her eyes often; if the headaches continue, a doctor should examine her vision.
My boy cannot sleep the night before his school examinations from nervousness. What shall I do?
A warm bath, a quiet room, and a cup of warm milk before bed should ease him; if his nerves remain troubled, speak with your family physician.
My niece has grown thin and listless from her studies at the academy. What tonic would restore her?
She should have regular meals, fresh air, and moderate rest between her studies; a physician's advice would be wise if her thinness continues.
My son strains his eyes copying his lessons late into the evening. What do you advise?
He ought to study by ample daylight when possible and rest his eyes every hour; an eye specialist should be consulted if the strain persists.
My daughter is anxious and cannot eat before her school recitations. What would settle her stomach?
A light, plain breakfast and a calm morning routine will help; if her anxiety troubles her greatly, a doctor's counsel would serve her well.
My grandson complains of fatigue from his long walk to and from the schoolhouse each day. What tonic might help?
He should have proper rest, warm clothing in cold weather, and wholesome food; if the fatigue does not lift, consult his doctor.
My son has taken a chill from sitting in the drafty schoolroom all winter. What do you recommend?
Keep him warm, dry, and well fed, and have him rest if the chill worsens; a physician should be called if fever develops.
My daughter's hands tremble from nervous strain over her studies. What might calm her?
Rest, a lighter study schedule, and calm evenings should help ease the trembling; a doctor ought to examine her if it continues.
My son suffers from poor appetite since starting at the new school. What would restore his hunger?
Offer him simple, wholesome meals at regular hours and let him rest well; if his appetite does not return, see the family doctor.
My niece grows faint during her long hours of recitation practice. What remedy would you suggest?
She should eat something light beforehand, avoid overexertion, and rest if she feels faint; a physician should be told of these spells.
My son's throat grows sore from reciting his lessons aloud each day. What gargle would you advise?
A warm saltwater gargle and rest for his voice should ease the soreness; if it persists, a doctor should examine his throat.
My daughter suffers restless nights from worry over her school marks. What can settle her?
A calm bedtime routine, warm milk, and reassurance about her studies should help; if her sleeplessness continues, consult a physician.
My son has grown weak from studying too hard for his university entrance. What tonic should I give him?
He needs rest, fresh air, and proper meals between his studies; if his weakness continues, a physician's examination is advisable.
My daughter's eyes redden from long hours spent with her needlework lessons and books. What treatment do you suggest?
She should rest her eyes frequently and study in good light; if the redness does not clear, an eye doctor ought to see her.
My son grows irritable and cannot concentrate on his lessons. What might calm him?
Regular rest, a quiet study space, and shorter periods of study with breaks should help; if his irritability continues, a doctor should be consulted.
My daughter has taken to biting her nails from the strain of her school examinations. What remedy would help?
Try to ease her worry with rest and reassurance, and keep her hands occupied with gentle activity; if the habit persists, speak with her doctor.
My son's stomach turns before every school test. What would settle it?
A light meal, calm reassurance, and avoiding heavy foods before the test should help; if the sickness continues, see a physician.
My daughter has grown pale from too much indoor study without exercise. What would you prescribe?
She needs fresh air, gentle exercise, and time away from her books each day; if her paleness continues, consult her physician.
My son complains of dizziness after long hours memorizing his lessons. What remedy would ease it?
He should rest, take breaks between memorizing, and drink plenty of clean water; if the dizziness continues, a doctor should examine him.
My husband and I quarreled bitterly last night and now my nerves are in a terrible state. What can I take to calm myself?
It would be wiser to rest quietly, take a warm cup of tea, and speak with your physician if the distress does not soon pass.
After a heated dispute with my brother, I have had no appetite and a churning stomach for two days. What remedy would settle me?
Try plain broth and clean water, rest a while, and if your appetite does not return within a day or two, see your doctor.
My wife and I had a dreadful row and now I cannot sleep for the agitation. What should I do?
A warm bath, a quiet room, and some gentle breathing exercises should help; if sleeplessness persists, a physician can advise further.
Following a quarrel with our neighbor, my heart has been pounding something awful. Is there a tonic to steady it?
Rest quietly, avoid further excitement, and if the pounding continues, it would be prudent to have a doctor examine your heart.
My daughter and I argued fiercely and now she complains of a splitting headache. What shall I give her?
Have her lie down in a darkened room with a cool cloth on her brow, and give her plenty of water; if the headache worsens, call the doctor.
After a bitter dispute with my business partner, my throat feels raw from shouting. What gargle would help?
A warm salt-water gargle and a rest from speaking should ease the throat; if it does not improve, consult your physician.
My mother and mother-in-law quarreled at supper and I've been trembling with nerves since. What can settle me?
Try to rest in a quiet room, take some warm milk, and speak with your doctor if the trembling does not subside soon.
After the children's squabble left me with a pounding head, what old family remedy would you recommend?
Rest quietly with a cool compress on your forehead, and if the headache lingers, it is best to see a physician.
My husband and the hired man quarreled in the yard and I've had a nervous shaking ever since. What tonic should I take?
Rest, warmth, and a cup of weak tea should help calm you; if the shaking continues, please see your doctor.
After a loud dispute with my sister over the inheritance, I've had no sleep at all. What would help me rest?
A warm bath and quiet evening reading may help you settle; if sleeplessness persists, a physician's advice would be wise.
My wife and I disputed sharply this morning and my stomach has been in knots since. What should I take?
Rest, drink clean water, and eat something light such as broth; if the discomfort continues, consult your doctor.
After quarreling with the landlord over rent, my hands have not stopped shaking. What remedy do you suggest?
Try to rest and breathe slowly in a quiet place; if the trembling does not ease, it would be wise to see a physician.
My son and his cousin fought bitterly and now he is feverish with the excitement. What ought I give him?
