Keep him quiet, warm, and give him plenty of clean water; if the fever does not break soon, please call the doctor.
After a heated argument at the market, my chest has felt tight and I cannot catch my breath easily. What would help?
Sit quietly, loosen your collar, and take slow breaths; if the tightness does not pass, please see a physician promptly.
My husband and the neighbor quarreled over the fence line and I've had terrible indigestion since. What can settle it?
Try plain warm water and a light meal, and rest a while; if the indigestion persists, consult your doctor.
After my daughter's quarrel with her intended, she has been weeping and cannot eat. What tonic would restore her appetite?
Encourage her to rest, take small sips of broth, and give her time to calm; if she does not improve, a physician should see her.
My brothers quarreled violently and one has taken a nervous fit since. What should we give him to calm down?
Keep him in a quiet, darkened room and speak to him gently; if the fit does not pass, send for the doctor at once.
After a dispute with my employer, I've had cold sweats and cannot steady my hands. What remedy would you advise?
Rest in a cool, quiet place and drink water slowly; if the sweating and shaking persist, please consult your doctor.
My wife and her sister quarreled fiercely and now I have a ringing in my ears from the shouting. What cure would you suggest?
Rest quietly away from noise for a day or two; if the ringing does not stop, it would be best to see a physician.
After quarreling with my father over the farm, I've felt faint and weak all afternoon. What would restore my strength?
Sit down, rest, and take some water and a light bite to eat; if the faintness continues, please see a doctor.
My aunt is coming to stay and complains of a nagging cough. What should I have ready for her?
Offer her a warm, well-ventilated room, plenty of clean water and rest, and suggest she see a physician if the cough persists or worsens.
A guest arriving this weekend has been feeling faint on the journey. How ought I revive her upon arrival?
Have her sit quietly, loosen any tight clothing, offer a little water, and let her rest until she feels steady; call a doctor if the faintness continues.
My husband's business partner is visiting and complains of a sore throat. What remedy should I offer him at supper?
Warm salted water for gargling, a soft diet, and a good night's rest are best; if the soreness lingers, he should consult a physician.
We have visitors with a fussy infant who won't sleep. What might I give the baby so the household can rest?
Try a warm, quiet room, gentle rocking, and a light feeding; if the child seems truly unwell, the parents should see a doctor rather than dose him themselves.
My elderly uncle is coming for the holiday and complains of weak spirits. What tonic shall I have ready for him?
Good food, fresh air, and cheerful company do more for weak spirits than any tonic; if he seems truly unwell, he ought to see his own doctor.
A neighbor's child is visiting and has broken out in a rash. Should I treat it before her mother arrives?
Keep the skin clean and dry, avoid any harsh applications, and let her mother or a doctor examine it properly when they arrive.
My sister is visiting with a headache from her long train ride. What should I give her for it?
A quiet, darkened room, a cool cloth on her brow, and a cup of weak tea should ease her; if the headache is severe or lasting, she should see a physician.
We are expecting guests, and one has written ahead that his stomach has been troubling him. What ought I prepare?
Plain, light food, clean boiled water, and rest are safest; if his stomach trouble continues, he should be seen by a doctor.
My mother-in-law arrives tomorrow with a persistent toothache. What can I offer her for the pain?
A cold compress against the cheek and a clove of oil applied sparingly may ease her until she can see a dentist promptly.
A visiting cousin seems short of breath after climbing our stairs. Should I give her something at once?
Have her sit and rest quietly in a well-aired room; if the shortness of breath does not pass, a doctor should be sent for.
We have a houseguest who cannot sleep in an unfamiliar bed. What might I offer to help him rest?
A quiet room, a warm blanket, and perhaps some warm milk without any medicine should help; persistent sleeplessness is best mentioned to a doctor.
My brother's family is visiting and one of the children has come down with a fever overnight. What shall I do before morning?
Keep the child cool, offer plenty of clean water, and send for the doctor without delay if the fever is high or does not break.
A dinner guest has taken ill suddenly with dizziness at our table. What should I give her right away?
Help her sit down, loosen her collar, and let her rest quietly with a little water; if the dizziness does not pass, call a physician.
My friend arriving for tea has mentioned her nerves have been poor lately. What should I have on hand for her?
A calm, pleasant visit, a cup of mild tea, and gentle conversation are best; if her nerves trouble her greatly, she should speak with her doctor.
We are hosting a guest recovering from a cold. Ought I dose him with something strong to speed his recovery?
Warmth, rest, and plenty of clean fluids serve recovery best; let him mend gradually and see a doctor if his cold worsens.
My visiting grandmother complains her joints ache from the journey. What remedy should I prepare?
A warm compress and a comfortable chair to rest in will ease her joints; persistent aching should be looked at by her physician.
A guest at our table has begun coughing badly during dinner. What should I fetch for him at once?
A glass of warm water and a moment to step away and rest should ease the coughing; if it continues, he ought to see a doctor.
My cousin's baby, visiting for the christening, has a slight fever. Should I dose him before the ceremony?
Keep the baby lightly dressed and cool, and if the fever does not ease soon, it is wisest to consult a doctor before proceeding.
A house guest has developed a persistent skin irritation from travel dust. What ointment should I offer?
Gentle washing with clean water and a mild, unscented lotion should soothe the skin; if it worsens, a doctor should examine it.
My uncle, visiting from the city, complains of exhaustion and asks for something to perk him up before dinner. What shall I serve?
A short rest, a light meal, and fresh air before dinner will do him more good than any tonic; if his exhaustion is unusual, he should see a physician.
My husband cannot fall asleep before midnight most nights. What would you suggest for him?
He might try a warm bath, a quiet room free of light, and a regular hour for retiring. If sleeplessness persists, he should see a physician to learn the cause.
Our baby fusses and will not settle at night. What household remedy would help her sleep?
Check that she is warm, dry, and well fed, and keep the nursery calm and dim. If her fussing continues, a doctor should examine her.
I toss and turn for hours before drifting off. Is there a tonic that might help?
A light supper, no strong tea or coffee in the evening, and a quiet, dark room often help. If wakefulness continues, do consult your physician.
My elderly father wakes several times through the night. What might ease his rest?
See that his room is warm and well ventilated and that he does not take fluids too late in the evening. A doctor should be consulted, as broken sleep in the aged can have many causes.
My son studies late and complains he cannot get to sleep afterward. What would you advise?
He should set his books aside an hour before bed, take a short walk, and keep to a steady bedtime. If his mind still races, a physician's advice would be wise.
My wife suffers from nightmares that leave her exhausted each morning. What household remedy do you recommend?
Rest, a calm evening routine, and avoiding heavy meals late at night may help. If the nightmares continue, she ought to see a doctor to be sure nothing else is amiss.
Our lodger complains of insomnia brought on by his nerves. What can we offer him?
A quiet room, warm milk before bed, and freedom from worry in the evening hours often help. He would do well to see a physician if his nerves remain troubled.
My little boy wakes crying in the night and cannot be settled. What would you suggest?
Check that he is not too warm or too cold, and comfort him gently until he calms. If the waking continues, a doctor should look him over.
I feel drowsy all day but cannot sleep properly at night. Is there a remedy?
Try to keep regular hours, take some fresh air and mild exercise by day, and avoid napping too long in the afternoon. If the trouble persists, see your physician.
My grandmother says she has not had a full night's rest in weeks. What can be done for her?
Warmth, quiet, and a light evening meal may help her rest better. Given her age, it would be wise to have a doctor examine her.
My husband works nights and cannot sleep well during the day. What household advice would you give?
Darkening the room heavily and keeping the household quiet during his rest hours will help greatly. If his sleep remains poor, a physician's counsel would be advisable.
My daughter is too excited to sleep before examinations. What might calm her for the night?
A calm evening, some quiet reading, and a warm bath before bed often settle young nerves. If she remains too restless, a doctor's advice would be sensible.
I have taken to lying awake worrying over household affairs. What remedy would help me sleep?
Setting worries aside with a short walk or quiet occupation before bed may help. If sleeplessness continues, it is best to speak with your physician.
My infant sleeps only in short spells and wakes often. What would you suggest we give her?
Ensure she is comfortable, fed, and not overheated, and keep her nights as quiet as possible. If her sleep does not improve, a physician should be consulted.
My brother suffers from restless legs that keep him from sleeping. What household treatment might ease this?
Gentle stretching, warmth, and avoiding strong tea in the evening may bring some relief. Persistent restlessness ought to be looked into by a doctor.
I find myself waking at three each morning and cannot return to sleep. What remedy do you recommend?
Try to keep a steady bedtime and avoid rich food late in the evening. If the early waking continues, your physician should be consulted.
My husband's snoring keeps the whole house from resting well. Is there something we might try?
Sleeping on his side and keeping the bedroom well aired may help somewhat. If the snoring is severe, a doctor should examine him.
My young niece walks in her sleep and it frightens the household. What should we do for her?
Keep her room safe and free of hazards, and see that she keeps regular, calm hours. It would be wise to have a physician look into the cause.
I am so fatigued by day yet restless by night. What would you advise for better rest?
Regular hours, mild exercise in daylight, and a calm evening routine often help restore proper rest. If fatigue and restlessness continue, please see your doctor.
My wife cannot sleep since our new baby arrived and looks quite worn. What remedy would help her rest?
She should try to rest when the baby sleeps and share night duties where possible to gain proper rest. If her exhaustion does not improve, a physician's visit is advisable.
My husband was caught in a cold autumn downpour and now shivers something dreadful. What ought I give him?
Get him into dry clothes and a warm bed, give him warm broth, and send for the doctor if fever or coughing sets in.
The children grow so listless in this summer heat—is there a tonic to perk them up?
Keep them in the shade with plenty of cool water and light clothing, and let them rest through the hottest part of the day.
My throat has been raw ever since that sharp autumn wind came through the valley. What shall I gargle with?
Gargle warm salted water and keep a scarf about your neck, and see a physician if the soreness does not ease in a few days.
The baby will not sleep with all this thunder and rain—what may I give her to settle her?
Keep the room dark and calm, hold her gently, and let her settle in her own time on her usual feeding schedule.
This spring dampness has set my knees to aching terribly—what rub do you recommend?
Keep the joints warm and dry, move about gently each day, and consult a doctor if the pain does not lessen.
My cheeks have gone quite pale through this long winter—how might I regain some color?
Take fresh air and modest exercise on fine winter days, and see that your meals are wholesome and regular.
This sudden cold snap has settled on my chest—what do you suggest to loosen it?
Try steam inhalations and a warm chest compress, rest well, and call the doctor should breathing grow difficult.
Every spring I fall into such a tiredness—is there something to give me vigor?
See that you sleep enough, eat well, and take a daily walk in the fresh spring air.
This winter cough of mine simply will not quit—what remedy would ease it?
Try warm honey and lemon drinks, keep the air in your room moist, and see a doctor if the cough lingers past a fortnight.
The cold weather has set my tooth to aching fiercely—what can I do until I reach the dentist?
Rinse with warm salt water and apply a warm compress to the jaw, then see the dentist as soon as you are able.
My hands have gone raw with chilblains from the winter cold—how might I treat them?
Keep the hands warm and dry, wear proper gloves outdoors, and rub in a mild soothing cream.
This sudden shift from warm to cold weather has left my nerves quite unsettled—what would calm me?
Rest quietly with a hot water bottle and a warm drink, and see a physician if the unease does not pass.
The summer heat has brought on a pounding headache—what relief would you advise?
Rest in a shaded, cool room with a damp cloth on the brow and drink plenty of water.
Every spring when the pollen rises my nose runs and my eyes water terribly—what treats hay fever best?
Keep windows closed against pollen where you can, rinse the nasal passages with mild saline, and see a doctor if it worsens.
This damp autumn air has settled on my chest something awful—what plaster might help?
Keep warm and dry, take some gentle steam inhalation, and rest until the chest clears.
My little boy has taken a heavy cough this winter—what syrup would you trust?
Give him warm fluids and keep the air moist, let him rest, and see a doctor should the cough grow worse.
The rainy season here always brings on a shaking fever—how much quinine should I take?
Rest, drink clean boiled water, and take only the quinine your doctor has prescribed, following his directions closely.
The dry cold of winter has left my skin cracked and itching—what ointment should I use?
Use a mild moisturizing cream, take warm rather than hot baths, and avoid harsh soap in the cold months.
Come every springtime my nose stuffs up something dreadful—what drops would you suggest?
Try steam inhalation and a gentle saline rinse, and rest until the congestion eases.
These short, dark winter days have left me terribly low in spirits—what would lift me?
Get what sunlight the season allows, eat warm nourishing meals, and keep close company with family; see a doctor if the low spirits persist.
My daughter's spotted complexion threatens her chances at the coming season's balls, and I fear for the family's good name—what shall restore her skin before then?
Have her wash gently with mild soap and rest well, and let a physician examine her, for such blemishes are often best treated with patience and proper diet.
My hands tremble so before my business partners that I fear it disgraces me—what remedy shall steady them?
Rest your nerves, avoid strong drink and coffee, and consult a physician to learn the true cause of the trembling.
My breath is foul and I dread the shame it brings at church socials—what shall I gargle to be rid of it?
Rinse with clean water after meals and see a dentist, for foul breath is often a sign of decay that wants proper care.
I cannot sleep for worry over my standing at the mill, and my nerves are quite frayed—what tonic shall calm me?
Take warm milk, quiet rest, and fresh air of an evening, and speak with your doctor if the worry persists.
My husband's snoring has become the talk of the neighborhood and shames our household—what cure shall silence him?
Have him seen by a physician, for loud snoring may point to a health matter best examined properly.
My son stammers so before the town council that I fear it disgraces our family name—what shall cure his tongue?
Encourage calm, patient practice at home, and consult a physician who may recommend a proper speech specialist.
I fainted at the church supper and now whispers follow me everywhere—what remedy shall strengthen my constitution?
Rest well, eat nourishing food, and let a physician examine you to discover the true cause of the fainting.
My baby's incessant crying at night has set the whole street gossiping about my fitness as a mother—what shall quiet her?
Keep her warm, fed, and gently soothed, and if the crying continues take her to a physician to be examined.
My gray hairs have come too soon, and my rivals whisper that I am past my prime—what shall restore the color quickly?
Care for your general health with good food and rest, for graying is natural and no cause for shame.
My rheumatism makes me limp before the men at the lodge, and I fear they think me feeble—what shall cure it swiftly?
Keep the joint warm and rested, and see a physician, for lasting relief comes from proper care, not haste.
I blush and sweat terribly whenever I speak in company, and it shames me before my peers—what draught shall calm me?
Practice calm, slow breathing beforehand, and speak with your doctor if the nervousness troubles you greatly.
My children have taken lice from school and I fear the shame it brings upon our household—what shall rid them quickly?
Wash the hair carefully with mild soap and a fine comb, and ask your doctor or pharmacist for a proper remedy.
My eyesight fails me, and I dread that spectacles will make me seem old and unfit for my post—what tonic shall restore it?
Have your eyes examined by a qualified doctor, and wear spectacles if he advises it, for clear sight matters more than vanity.
I limp from an old injury and fear the veterans think me unfit for honour among them—what remedy shall mend my leg?
Rest the leg, keep it warm, and let a physician examine it properly before attempting any cure.
My melancholy spells have become known about town, and I fear they call me weak of will—what tonic shall lift my spirits?
Rest, take fresh air and simple exercise, and speak honestly with a physician about your low spirits.
My toothache has left me unable to smile in society, and I fear my reputation suffers for it—what shall ease the pain?
A dab of clove oil may ease the pain temporarily, but see a dentist promptly to have it properly treated.
I suffer such flatulence at dinner parties that I dread the ridicule it brings—what remedy shall settle my stomach?
Eat plainly and slowly, drink warm water after meals, and consult your doctor if the trouble continues.
My pale, sickly look has cost me a suitor's good opinion of my vigor—what tonic shall bring color to my cheeks quickly?
Spend time in the fresh air, eat well, and rest properly, and let a physician check that nothing more serious ails you.
My weeping sores upon my hands shame me before my customers—what wash shall clear them at once?
Keep the hands clean and bandaged gently, and have a physician examine the sores to ensure proper healing.
My weight has fallen away and the town whispers I am consumptive, ruining my good name—what shall restore my flesh?
Rest well, eat nourishing food, take fresh air, and see a physician promptly to learn the true cause of the loss.
My uncle's estate has been tied up in probate for months and the worry keeps me from sleeping. What might I take to settle my nerves of a night?
Try a cup of warm milk, a quiet room, and regular hours of rest; if the sleeplessness persists, do consult your physician.
Since Father's will was read and the children fell to quarreling over the farm, I have suffered terrible headaches. What do you advise?
Rest in a darkened room, apply a cool cloth to the brow, and if the headaches continue, see a qualified doctor.
Settling Grandfather's property has left me utterly worn and nervous. Is there a tonic that might restore my strength?
Plenty of rest, fresh air, and simple nourishing food will do more good than any tonic; a physician's advice is wise if weakness lingers.
I have taken a sore throat from the journey to settle the land dispute with my cousins. What do you recommend?
A gargle of warm salt water, rest for the voice, and plenty of warm drink should ease it; see a doctor if it does not improve.
The worry over my late aunt's inheritance has left my complexion sallow and drawn. What might restore it?
Good food, sound sleep, and fresh air are the surest cure for a worn complexion; consult a doctor if you remain unwell.
The quarrel over Grandmother's house has upset my stomach terribly. What ought I take for it?
A bland diet, boiled water, and rest are best for an unsettled stomach; if it does not pass, see a physician.
The baby has been fretful and teething while the family waits on the reading of the will. What may I give her?
A cool teething ring and a calm, quiet room will comfort her best; if she seems truly unwell, take her to the doctor.
Since learning I was left less than my brothers, my heart has taken to fluttering strangely. What is the remedy?
Rest quietly, avoid excitement and strong drink, and have a doctor examine your heart to be certain all is well.
I caught a chill traveling to settle my late aunt's estate and now have a nagging cough. What should I do?
Warm fluids, rest, and a warm room are the best remedy for a cough; if it lingers, a doctor should be consulted.
Ever since my brother contested Father's will, I have fallen into low spirits and cannot shake them. What tonic would help?
Sunlight, gentle exercise, and good company do much for low spirits; if the melancholy persists, a physician's help is wise.
The long dispute over the farmland inheritance has left me weak and listless. What might restore my strength?
Nutritious meals, ample rest, and fresh air will restore your strength better than any tonic; see a doctor if the weakness continues.
Grief over Mother's passing and the wrangling over her property have made my gums sore and tender. What should I use?
A gentle rinse of warm salt water and soft brushing should ease the soreness; if it does not improve, see a dentist.
The endless meetings with lawyers over Grandfather's estate have left my nerves quite frayed. What would calm them?
A cup of chamomile tea, quiet rest, and steady breathing will do much to calm the nerves; consult a doctor if the strain continues.
The strain of dividing the family silver among us has brought out a troublesome rash on my hands. What is the cure?
Mild soap, clean water, and keeping the hands dry should help the rash; if it worsens, see a physician.
I took a fever on the long journey to claim my share of the inheritance. What should be done for it?
Cool cloths, plenty of water, and quiet rest are the proper treatment for fever; send for a doctor without delay.
My son cannot sleep since the family began arguing over who shall keep the house. What might help him rest?
A warm bath, a quiet room, and a calm bedtime routine will help him rest; if the trouble continues, consult a doctor.
Since being told I was left out of the will entirely, I have suffered fainting spells. What is the remedy?
Lie down at once when faint, keep cool and rest, and have a physician look into the cause of the spells.
Settling my uncle's property in this cold weather has left me with a persistent cough. What do you suggest?
A warm compress on the chest, plenty of rest, and warm drinks should ease the cough; see a doctor if it does not clear.
My tooth has ached fiercely all through these stressful estate meetings. What might soothe it?
A warm salt water rinse may ease the discomfort for a time, but you should see a dentist as soon as possible.
I have had no appetite at all since the inheritance dispute began. What would you recommend to bring it back?
Simple, nourishing broths and small regular meals often help restore the appetite; if it does not return, consult a physician.
My daughter is to be married next month and frets herself sleepless over the arrangements. What may I give her for her nerves?
Encourage her to rest, take gentle walks, and eat simply; if her nerves remain troubled, a family physician can advise a safe remedy.
The bride wishes her complexion to be perfectly pale and clear for the ceremony. What do you suggest?
Good rest, plenty of water, and mild soap and water washing will keep her complexion healthy and naturally clear.
My son is to be wed soon but complains of low vigor and fears he will not be equal to married life. What tonic would you recommend?
He should ensure proper rest, good food, and moderate exercise, and consult a physician if his fatigue persists.
The groom has taken a chill from standing about at the church rehearsal in the cold. How ought we treat it?
Warmth, rest, and a hot drink should ease the chill; if fever develops, a doctor should be sent for.
My niece is to be married and suffers terribly from wedding-day jitters and a nervous stomach. What remedy would settle her?
A light meal, calm surroundings, and a few deep breaths should help; if her distress is severe, a physician's advice is wise.
The bridegroom has a persistent cough that worries the family before the wedding trip. What would you advise?
Rest, warm fluids, and avoiding chill should ease the cough; a doctor should examine him if it lingers.
My daughter cannot sleep for excitement the week before her wedding. Is there something safe to quiet her mind at night?
Warm milk, a quiet room, and a settled evening routine will help her rest; persistent sleeplessness should be discussed with a doctor.
The bride's mother suffers from headaches brought on by all the wedding preparations. What relief can you suggest?
Rest in a darkened room, plenty of water, and a lighter workload should ease her headaches; a physician can help if they continue.
My future son-in-law has weak digestion and worries it will trouble him at the wedding breakfast. What do you recommend?
Simple, light food and eating slowly should help his digestion; if trouble persists, he ought to see a doctor beforehand.
The young bride has fainted twice while fitting her wedding gown. What is the cause and cure?
She may simply be overtired or laced too tightly; loosening her garments, rest, and fresh air should help, with a doctor consulted if fainting continues.
My son is anxious about his wedding night and asks what may calm his nerves beforehand.
A calm evening, plain conversation, and simple reassurance are best; there is no need for any medicine at all.
The bride's skin has broken out just before the wedding and she is distressed. What treatment would clear it quickly?
Gentle washing, plenty of rest, and avoiding rich foods will help most; persistent skin trouble should be shown to a doctor.
My daughter has caught a cold just days before her wedding and fears she will lose her voice for the vows. What should she take?
Rest, warm drinks, and keeping warm should help; if her voice does not return, a doctor should be consulted promptly.
The groom's mother is exhausted from wedding preparations and cannot keep up her strength. What tonic would restore her?
Rest, good meals, and a lighter share of duties will restore her strength best; a doctor's advice is wise if fatigue continues.
My niece, soon to be married, has swollen feet from standing at fittings. What relief can be given her?
Resting with her feet raised, cool cloths, and shorter fitting sessions should ease the swelling.
The bride is troubled by a nervous rash on her wedding morning. What ointment would you suggest?
A cool compress and avoiding harsh soaps should soothe the rash; if it worsens, a physician should be seen at once.
My son, the groom, has lost his appetite entirely from nerves before the wedding. What would restore it?
Small, plain meals and calm surroundings often restore appetite; if he continues to eat poorly, a doctor should be consulted.
The bride's grandmother suffers palpitations from the excitement of the wedding preparations. What would settle her heart?
She should rest quietly and avoid overexertion; any heart palpitations ought to be examined by a physician promptly.
My daughter has developed a fever the night before her wedding. Ought we dose her heavily to see her through the ceremony?
She should rest in bed with light covers and plenty of water; a doctor ought to see her before any decision is made about the ceremony.
The groom's best man has a toothache troubling him the day before the wedding. What quick remedy would you advise?
A cold compress on the cheek and a visit to the dentist as soon as possible would be the sensible course.
My mother cannot sleep since we buried my father last week; what can I give her of an evening?
Warm milk, quiet company, and gentle occupation by day will serve her better than any drug; if her sleeplessness persists, she ought to see the doctor.
My little girl has gone pale and will not eat since her grandmother's funeral—what shall I do?
Let her rest, take simple broths and plenty of clean water, and if she does not mend within a few days, have the doctor call.
One of the mourners fainted dead away at the wake—how ought we revive such spells?
Loosen her collar, lay her flat with her feet raised, and give her air and quiet; call the doctor if she does not soon come round.
I have sat up three nights at the coffin-side and feel quite worn; what restorative would you suggest?
You must take turns with others so as to sleep properly, eat regular meals, and rest — no tonic can substitute for that.
My husband stood bareheaded in the rain at the graveside and has taken a chill; how shall we treat it?
Get him into dry, warm clothes, put him to bed with warm drinks, and send for the doctor should fever or cough develop.
There has been a death from fever in the house—how should we cleanse the sickroom before the funeral guests arrive?
Air the room thoroughly, wash surfaces with a mild disinfectant solution as the doctor advises, and let sunlight in for several days.
My throat is raw and my head aches from weeping through the funeral service; what remedy would ease it?
A warm salt-water gargle, plenty of rest, and warm drinks should ease it; see the doctor if the soreness lingers.
My aunt, quite elderly, grew faint and weak from standing so long through my uncle's service—what tonic would restore her strength?
She should rest in bed a day or two with nourishing broth and clean water, and be seen by the doctor if her weakness does not pass.
The baby has been fretful and will not settle since the household went into mourning—what shall we do for her?
Keep to her usual feeding and sleeping times as best you can, keep her warm and comforted, and consult the doctor if her fretfulness continues.
My wife grew faint in her black mourning dress at the graveside in the heat—how should we care for her?
Loosen her stays, bring her into the shade with air and water, and let her rest quietly; if the fainting recurs, have the doctor examine her.
I am quite spent from arranging my brother's funeral all week—what restorative do you recommend?
You need proper sleep, regular meals, and a little rest each day; no tonic will serve so well as that.
My sister has taken no proper meal in three weeks since we buried her son—how may we tempt her appetite back?
Offer her small, simple meals frequently, encourage gentle walks in the air, and have the doctor see her if her appetite does not return.
My throat has gone quite hoarse from crying through two days of wake and burial—what should I take for it?
Rest your voice, sip warm tea with honey, and let the throat heal on its own; see a doctor if the hoarseness persists.
We are anxious lest viewing my uncle's body has exposed the family to some contagion—what precaution should we take?
If the cause of death was not contagious, there is little cause for alarm; keep the household clean and well-rested, and consult the doctor with any worry.
My nerves are quite shattered since my husband's burial—what tonic will settle them?
Quiet rest, simple food, and the company of friends will do more for your nerves than any tonic; a doctor's visit would also be wise.
My son is frightened and cannot sleep since he attended his grandfather's funeral—what shall I give him?
Sit with him a while at bedtime, speak gently of his grandfather, and keep his evenings calm; if his fright does not ease, the doctor may help.
My father walked the whole funeral procession in a cold downpour and now coughs badly—what remedy should we use?
Keep him warm and dry indoors, give him plenty of fluids, and send for the doctor if the cough worsens or fever sets in.
My eyes are swollen and sore from weeping so much this past week of mourning—what remedy would you suggest?
A cool, clean cloth held gently to the eyes and plenty of rest should ease the swelling; see a doctor if soreness continues.
We fear the 'bad air' left in the house since my mother's death still lingers—how should we clear it?
Open the windows wide and let fresh air circulate through the house for several days; there is no need for harsher measures.
I have been sunk in melancholy for weeks now since we laid my daughter to rest—what remedy will lift my spirits?
Time, the comfort of family, gentle activity, and rest will help you through this grief; if the melancholy does not lift, please see a doctor.
